consuming_steps: 2.1 (Failure of fixed-Sobolev continuity on smooth modes.) Fix $\tau>0$ and an integer $r\ge0$. In step 1.1 take $A_n=(1+n^2)^{-r/2}e^{-an\tau/2}$. Under the derivative-sum norm of [L3], $\|\cos(nx^1)\|_{H^r}^2=\tfrac12\sum_{j=0}^r n^{2j}$, which lies between positive constants times $(1+n^2)^r$, uniformly for $n\ge1$. Consequently the initial H^r norm tends to zero, whereas the density H^r norm at $\tau$ is at least a positive constant times $e^{an\tau/2}$ and tends to infinity. Each datum and solution is a single trigonometric polynomial and hence smooth; indeed the data tend to zero in every fixed derivative norm because exponential decay dominates every power. Any other classical solution of the same datum has the same coefficient at $(n,0,0)$ by step 1.1. For any such density lying in $H^r$, integration by parts gives $n^r|\widehat f(n,0,0)|=|\widehat{D_1^rf}(n,0,0)|\le\|D_1^rf\|_2\le\|f\|_{H^r}$. The coefficient inequality follows from $|\widehat h(k)|\le\int|h|\le\|h\|_2$; the second bound follows by expanding $0\le\int(|h|-\int|h|)^2$ on the normalized probability space. Consequently every classical solution choice has density $H^r$ norm at least a positive constant times $e^{an\tau/2}$. Thus no choice of a solution operator, even restricted to these smooth trigonometric data, can be continuous at zero from $H^r$ data to $H^r$ values at any fixed positive time. [step 1.1, L3, construct, algebra]

2.2 (A genuinely smooth datum with no linearized Sobolev solution.) Set $f_0(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-\sqrt n}\cos(nx^1)$ and $v_0=0$. For every integer $q\ge0$, $\sum_{n\ge1}n^qe^{-\sqrt n}<\infty$: group the terms with $j^2\le n<(j+1)^2$, whose contribution is at most $(2j+1)(j+1)^{2q}e^{-j}$, a summable polynomial times a geometric sequence. Thus each spatial derivative series converges uniformly; the fundamental theorem of calculus applied to partial sums and their uniformly convergent derivative series shows successively that $f_0$ is smooth with those derivatives. Suppose a periodic $C^1$ linearized solution existed on $[0,\tau]$. At each Fourier frequency $k$, differentiation under the integral and periodic integration by parts give $g_k'= -H_0 i k\cdot w_k$ and $H_0w_k'=a^2 i k g_k$. Thus $g_k$ is $C^2$ with $g_k''=a^2|k|^2g_k$. The explicit initial coefficients and zero velocity, together with uniqueness of this elementary ODE, force its coefficient at $(n,0,0)$ to be $\tfrac12e^{-\sqrt n}\cosh(an t)$. For every $t>0$ these coefficients tend to infinity, since $an t-\sqrt n\to\infty$, whereas every Fourier coefficient of the continuous density at that fixed time has absolute value at most $\int|f(t,x)|\,d\mu\le\sup_x|f(t,x)|<\infty$. This contradiction excludes a periodic classical solution on every positive time interval, without requiring an unproved inference from coefficient summability. This explicit datum is smooth; polynomially decaying coefficients of a fixed order would not have established that assertion. [step 1.1, L2, L3, construct, algebra]

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $s\ge0$ be an integer, and let
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $\mu$, $\chi_k$,
$\widehat u(k)$, the weak derivatives $D^\alpha$ and the spaces
$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be as in
[[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]], and put
$$N_s(u)^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|k|^2)^s\,|\widehat u(k)|^2,\qquad |k|^2:=k_1^2+k_2^2+k_3^2 .$$

[L1] $(\chi_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$ is an orthonormal basis of the complex $L^2$: for $f,g\in L^2$ one has the norm and pairing identities $\|f\|_2^2=\sum_k|\widehat f(k)|^2$ and $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_k\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$, the series converging absolutely, and the coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3)$ ([[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], [[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]]).

[L2] $v=D^\alpha u$ means $\int u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int v\,\varphi\,d\mu$ for every smooth test function $\varphi$; the real and imaginary parts of $\chi_l$ are smooth real tests; adding their test identities extends the identity complex-linearly to $\chi_l$ ([[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]]).

consuming_steps: 1.1 (One-variable periodic integration by parts.) For smooth $2\pi$-periodic $G,H$ and each $j$, $\int_{\mathbb T_{2\pi}}G\,\partial_jH\,d\mu_{\mathbb T}=-\int_{\mathbb T_{2\pi}}(\partial_jG)\,H\,d\mu_{\mathbb T}$: indeed $\int_0^{2\pi}\partial_j(GH)\,dx_j=(GH)|_0^{2\pi}=0$ by the second fundamental theorem of calculus and periodicity [L3], and the product rule gives the claim; the remaining coordinates integrate out by the product-measure convention. Consequently, for every smooth $\varphi$, every $k$ and every $\alpha$, $\int \chi_kD^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}(ik)^\alpha\int\chi_k\varphi\,d\mu$: induct on $|\alpha|$, moving one variable derivative from $\varphi$ onto $\chi_k$ by the one-variable identity and using $\partial_j\chi_k=ik_j\chi_k$. In particular $D^\alpha\chi_k=(ik)^\alpha\chi_k$ in the weak sense of [L2], the case $\varphi=\chi_{-l}$ tested against $\chi_k$ having Fourier coefficients $\widehat{\chi_k}(l)=\delta_{kl}$. [L2, L3, algebra]

2.1 (The differentiation identity (a).) If $u\in H^s$ and $|\alpha|\le s$, then $D^\alpha u\in H^{s-|\alpha|}$: a weak derivative of $D^\alpha u$ of order $|\beta|\le s-|\alpha|$ is the weak derivative $D^{\alpha+\beta}u$, because the defining test identity for the iterated derivative follows by applying the two defining identities in succession and noting that $D^\beta\varphi$ is again a smooth test function. Testing the defining identity for $D^\alpha u$ against $\varphi=\chi_{-k}$ gives $\widehat{D^\alpha u}(k)=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int u\,D^\alpha\chi_{-k}\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}(-ik)^\alpha\int u\,\chi_{-k}\,d\mu=(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)$, where the middle equality uses step 1.1 for the smooth test function $D^\alpha\chi_{-k}=(-ik)^\alpha\chi_{-k}$ and the last uses $(-1)^{|\alpha|}(-i)^\alpha=i^\alpha$. [step 1.1, L2, algebra]

2.2 (The norm bounds for $u\in H^s$.) By Parseval [L1] applied to the $L^2$ classes $D^\alpha u$, $\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2=\sum_k|k^\alpha|^2|\widehat u(k)|^2$, so the definition of the $H^s$ norm gives $\|u\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_kq_k|\widehat u(k)|^2$. Combining with step 1.2, $\|u\|_{H^s}^2\le(s+1)^3N_s(u)^2$ and $N_s(u)^2\le4^s\|u\|_{H^s}^2$, which are the right-hand inequality and the converse inequality of (b) whenever $u\in H^s$. [step 1.2, L1, algebra]

3.1 (Converse direction of (b): the weighted series produce weak derivatives.) Let $u\in L^2$ with $N_s(u)<\infty$. For each $|\alpha|\le s$ the sequence $k\mapsto(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)$ is square-summable because $|k^\alpha|^2\le(1+|k|^2)^{|\alpha|}\le(1+|k|^2)^s$; by the surjectivity of the coefficient isometry [L1] there is a unique class $w_\alpha\in L^2$ with $\widehat{w_\alpha}(k)=(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)$. Since $u$ is real, $\widehat u(-k)=\overline{\widehat u(k)}$ by conjugating its integral. Thus $a_k:=(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)$ satisfies $a_{-k}=\overline{a_k}$. Also $\widehat{\overline{w_\alpha}}(k)=\overline{\widehat{w_\alpha}(-k)}=a_k$, again by conjugating the integral. Injectivity in [L1] gives $\overline{w_\alpha}=w_\alpha$ as $L^2$ classes, so $w_\alpha$ has a real-valued representative, componentwise. Hence $D^\alpha u=w_\alpha$ weakly for every $|\alpha|\le s$, so $u\in H^s$. [step 2.1, L1, L2, algebra]

Smooth cutoff extension in the proved supplier gives these estimates on the actual compact value sets without assuming convexity. 1.2 ($L^2$ uniqueness for all stated classical solutions.) Set $E_0(t)=\int w^{\mathsf T}a w$. Symmetry and integration by parts give $E_0'=\int w^{\mathsf T}(\dot a+\partial_i a_i)w+2\int w^{\mathsf T}f$. Pointwise coefficient Lipschitz bounds give $|f|\le C|w|$, since $\partial_tv$ and $\partial_i v$ are bounded in $L^\infty$. Thus $|E_0'|\le CE_0$. If $w(0)=0$, Gronwall on either oriented segment from $0$ to $t$ gives $E_0(t)=0$. As $t\in J$ was arbitrary, this proves (a). [L1, L2, L3, L4, L5, algebra]

1.3 (Energy identity at the stated regularity.) Work on any compact time segment and define $E=\sum_{|\alpha|\le r}\int(D^\alpha w)^{\mathsf T}aD^\alpha w$. Put $w_N=P_Nw$, $h=\partial_tw$, and $y_\alpha=D^\alpha w$, $h_\alpha=D^\alpha h$. Classical $C^1$ regularity makes each Fourier coefficient $C^1$ with derivative the coefficient of $h$, so $w_N$ is a $C^1$ finite-dimensional curve. The bounds $w\in H^{r+1}$ and $h\in H^r$ are uniform at every time: the former is assumed and the latter follows pointwise from the PDE and [L4]. The tail bound [L6] gives uniform $L^2$ convergence $P_Ny_\alpha\to y_\alpha$ at rate $O((1+N^2)^{-1/2})$ since $y_\alpha\in H^1$ uniformly. Hence $E_N\to E$ uniformly. Finite-dimensional differentiation gives $E_N'=\sum_\alpha[2\langle P_Nh_\alpha,aP_Ny_\alpha\rangle+\langle P_Ny_\alpha,\dot aP_Ny_\alpha\rangle]$. By self-adjointness the first pairing equals $\langle h_\alpha,P_N(aP_Ny_\alpha)\rangle$. The quadratic terms also converge uniformly. Thus $E_N'$ converges uniformly to $G=\sum_\alpha[2\langle h_\alpha,ay_\alpha\rangle+\langle y_\alpha,\dot ay_\alpha\rangle]$. Integrating the scalar identities $E_N(t)-E_N(t')=\int_{t'}^tE_N'$ and passing uniformly to the limit gives $E(t)-E(t')=\int_{t'}^tG$; $G$ is continuous as a uniform limit of continuous functions. Therefore $E'=G$. The differentiated difference equation is an $L^2$ identity because $w\in H^{r+1}$ and $h\in H^r$; spatial integration by parts is justified by Fourier density and the $H^1$ bounds for $y_\alpha$. It may therefore be substituted into $G$ without additional time regularity assumptions. [L1, L3, L4, L6, algebra]

Choose a coordinate ball $B\Subset U$ meeting $\Sigma\cap U$ and cut off the data and the coefficient functions outside $B$; the resulting system is a periodic symmetric hyperbolic system after identifying a neighborhood of $B$ with an open subset of $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and extending by constants. By [L2] it has a smooth solution on a time interval around $0$; by the finite-speed independence clause of [L2], restricted to the domain of dependence of $\Sigma\cap B$ the solution depends only on the data and coefficients inside the patch, so the local solutions on overlapping balls agree and patch to a solution of $S(u)=0$ on a neighborhood $V$ of $\Sigma\cap U$.
